name: oe-kimi-F-S-P
finalResponse:
A supplement is the only product whose customer assumes it's lying before it speaks. Food nourishes, medicine cures — the supplement promises something in between, and "in between" is precisely where skepticism lives. So I'd gently push back on the brief's framing. "Ethical and effective" suggests a tradeoff to be managed. In this category they're the same move: the smallest claim you can prove will outperform the largest one you can't, because the first compounds and the second merely spikes. Perhaps the question isn't *how do we advertise this* but *how do we become believable in a category that has already spent its credibility.*

**The market: choose the strictest room.** Japan, if it were mine to choose — and I'd choose on exactly that logic. Take the market where exaggeration is not merely distrusted but illegal. Function claims must be filed with the Consumer Affairs Agency under the FFC system; disease language is forbidden outright; stealth marketing has been a punishable offense since 2023; and the subscription-trap scandals of the last decade left scar tissue that shoppers still check for. A market that has written its skepticism into law is a gift, really — the regulations are a map of exactly where trust was broken. And the culture already holds the concept the product needs: *me-byo*, the state between health and illness, where kampo tradition has located the real work of well-being for centuries. Supplements are inherently a me-byo product. Most markets make you explain that. This one already knows. (Were the market Germany or Brazil, the idioms would change. The shape wouldn't.)

**The positioning: own the in-between.** Not wellness, not treatment — the space between, where people actually live. The line should read two ways, as always: to the regulator, compliant; to the skeptic, honest. Something in the register of *"for the days between checkups."* The exact words matter less than that a pharmacist could repeat them without wincing and a regulator would nod. What you're claiming is not an outcome but a posture — maintenance, attention, the quiet work. It is a strangely defensible position, because no competitor can out-claim modesty without looking foolish.

**Say less; show the proof.** Here is the creative idea, and I'd suggest it's the only one contrarian enough to be believed: every piece of communication opens with what the product *won't* do. The list is longer, and we read it first. Then publish everything — the study, the dose rationale, the sourcing, who should *not* take it, what it interacts with. Boring is credible. Adjectives are not. Retire, or let fall quiet: "boost," "miracle," urgency of any kind, before-and-after imagery, and above all fear — fear converts once, trust repeats. This matters doubly in a market whose wound is precisely fear sold to the elderly. So: market to the family, never to the fear. The buyer and the taker are often different people — an adult daughter purchasing for a parent in another prefecture. Apply what you might call the daughter test: would she feel *respected* by this ad, or managed? She is the one who will notice.

**Be discovered, not announced.** The brand speaking about itself is suspect; others speaking about it is evidence. Cede the telling to the people the culture already trusts with such things — pharmacists at the drugstore counter, registered dietitians — and educate them deeply rather than paying them loudly. Where you do partner with creators, label it in a way that's almost ostentatious: *PR*, plain as day. The stealth-marketing rule is a compliance burden to everyone else and a trust asset to you, if you wear it visibly. Anchor the calendar to the checkup rhythm — the annual *ningen dock*, the ritual of knowing one's numbers — and sponsor the *knowing*, never the fixing. Give people a way to understand themselves and let the product sit adjacent to the knowledge rather than posing as the answer to it. A LINE channel that answers questions honestly, including "you probably don't need this," will do more than any campaign.

**Sequence it as drift, not launch.** First, before anything: audit whether the product deserves the story. No amount of cultural sensitivity repairs a molecule that doesn't work, and the FFC filing will force the question anyway — better to ask it yourself, earlier. Then a year of quiet: professional education, seeding, the archive of evidence made public, no manifesto. What you're waiting for is the earned question — the unprompted pharmacist recommendation, the review-site pickup you didn't arrange. That is the *tokuho* mark of the street, and it cannot be bought, only waited for. Measure pull, not reach: repeat rate above all — a supplement is a promise renewed monthly, so retention is the only honest metric — plus organic search and complaint lines as tripwires. Never announce a moment. Let someone else notice it.

**Make the ethics concrete, or it will evaporate.** "Do no harm" is unanswerable in the abstract, which is why it answers nothing. So: one page, three columns — *what we'll say, what we'll say only when asked, what we'll never say.* People argue far less once the claims have names. And give custody of the copy to your fiercest internal skeptic — the scientist, the regulatory counsel, whoever winces most at adjectives. They'll keep everyone honest, and their signature on the work is worth more than their objections ever cost. Two guardrails more: cancellation must be as easy as purchase — the cancel button is an advertisement for your character — and never target by health anxiety, however well the data allows it. Ask the brands that promised immune "boosting" in 2020 how the spike compared to the warning letters. The letters lasted longer.

If I were starting anywhere, I'd start with the first thousand buyers — the ones who came without being chased. What do they believe they're buying, I wonder? It usually isn't the molecule. And I'd want to know what the pharmacist at the counter says about the category when no one from the brand is listening. That answer, I'd suspect, is the whole campaign.
